meta.mbti_to_big_five: E/I maps mostly onto Extraversion, S/N onto Openness, T/F onto Agreeableness, J/P onto Conscientiousness [MC1989]. The MBTI has no Neuroticism scale. The T/F and J/P links are weaker than the other two, so a type derived from Big Five scores is an approximation.
meta.growth_caveat: Effects in these studies are small to moderate, mostly self-reported, and come from people who wanted to change. Evidence is strongest for emotional stability and Extraversion and weakest for Openness and Agreeableness [R2017]. The example tasks are written for this app in the style of the studies' challenges; they are not quoted from the papers.

how_celebs_are_typed: These types are popular guesses, not test results. I could not find any of these people's official MBTI results, and only one of the 42 has stated a type in public: Ray Dalio, who wrote 'I'm an ENTP' on X in 2018. Everything else comes from fans voting or writers speculating from interviews and public behaviour. The main source is the Personality Database (personality-database.com), where anyone can vote on a public figure's type and the top-voted type is shown. That site could not be read directly during this research, so its typings were taken from an open, undated snapshot on GitHub (AKAazure/character-personality-database) and from personalitylist.com, which carries the same typings (it matched the snapshot in all 10 cases checked). Neither gives vote counts, and live votes may have moved since. Editorial sites (JobCannon, Truity) and the small Sakinorva vote databank were used as cross-checks; they often disagree. 'Strong consensus' means the Personality Database type was found and no other source checked contradicted it (single_source marks cases with nothing independent to compare). 'Disputed' means sources disagree or the type differs from the label the app already shows. Public personas are curated, so treat all of this as entertainment.

INTJ.line: Works out where things should be in five years, then quietly builds the plan to get there.

growth.text: Pick one small social action a week, such as starting a short conversation with a colleague you rarely speak to, and tick it off. In a 15-week study, students who actually completed weekly challenges like this rose in Extraversion; those who signed up and did not follow through went slightly backwards.

Practise one warm act a day for three months: thank someone specifically, or ask a question before giving your view. A three-month coaching app built on daily micro-tasks moved people's chosen traits, and friends and family noticed the change.

INTP.line: Likes taking ideas apart to see how they work, and would rather be accurate than quick.

growth.text: Turn finishing into if-then plans: 'If it is 9am, then I spend 25 minutes on the task I am avoiding.' Specific if-then plans helped people change in the direction they wanted over 16 weeks, while vague intentions did not.
Share one half-formed idea out loud each week instead of waiting until it is perfect. Completing small weekly Extraversion challenges predicted real trait change over 15 weeks.

ENTJ.line: Sees what needs doing, organises people around it and expects results.

growth.text: In one meeting a day, summarise the other person's point to their satisfaction before you reply. Daily micro-tasks like this, kept up for three months through a coaching app, shifted chosen traits including Agreeableness.

Each week, complete one small act of trust or generosity, for example handing over a task without checking it. Trait change tracked the number of weekly challenges people finished, not the number they planned.

ENTP.line: Enjoys testing ideas by arguing with them, and is happiest when starting something new.

growth.text: Choose one unfinished project and set a weekly challenge you can tick off, such as 'ship the dull last 10% by Friday'. Completed challenges predicted gains in Conscientiousness; abandoned ones predicted a small drop.
Write an if-then plan for disagreements: 'If I am about to argue the opposite side, then I first say what I agree with.' If-then plans were the ingredient that helped wanted change happen.

INFJ.line: Reads people well, cares about doing the right thing and prefers a few deep relationships.

growth.text: Once a week, state a preference or say no in a low-stakes setting, such as choosing the restaurant. Assertiveness is part of Extraversion, and small completed challenges added up to trait change over 15 weeks.

Use a daily prompt for three months to start one conversation you would normally wait for. In the PEACH app trial, people who wanted to increase a trait changed, and the change was still there three months later.

INFP.line: Guided by personal values and imagination, and needs work that feels meaningful.

growth.text: Attach routine tasks to a cue: 'If I finish breakfast, then I clear my inbox for 15 minutes.' People with concrete if-then plans changed more than those with good intentions alone.
Pick one small weekly step towards being more outgoing, such as posting your work or voicing an opinion in a group, and record that you did it.

ENFJ.line: Brings people together, notices what each person needs and likes to see others do well.

growth.text: Your four letters sit at the high end of the traits they map onto, and the MBTI has no scale for emotional stability. Check your Big Five Neuroticism score in this app instead: it is the trait that responds most to intervention (about half a standard deviation across 207 studies).
If you set a change goal, choose one and finish it. People who accepted challenges and did not complete them moved in the wrong direction, so fewer commitments kept is better than many started.

ENFP.line: Full of ideas and energy, connects easily with people and dislikes routine.

growth.text: Take one weekly Conscientiousness challenge that is almost too easy, such as arriving five minutes early or tidying one surface, and tick it off. Completion, not ambition, predicted change.
Use a daily two-minute planning check-in for three months. The PEACH trial used short daily tasks and reflection, and increases were confirmed by people who knew the participants.

ISTJ.line: Reliable and thorough, trusts what has been shown to work and keeps promises.

growth.text: Try one unfamiliar thing a week, such as a different route, cuisine or type of book, and note what you thought of it. App-based daily tasks moved Openness goals too, though the wider evidence for Openness is weaker than for other traits.
Complete one small social challenge a week, such as asking a colleague about their weekend. Finished challenges predicted higher Extraversion after 15 weeks.

ISFJ.line: Quietly looks after people and details, and remembers what matters to others.

growth.text: Practise speaking up: once a week, give your opinion before being asked. Assertiveness sits within Extraversion, which rose for people who completed weekly challenges.
Write an if-then plan for novelty: 'If I am invited to something new, then I say yes once this month.' If-then plans turned a wish to change into measurable change.

ESTJ.line: Gets things organised, sets clear rules and makes sure the work is done properly.

growth.text: For three months, do one daily act that puts the relationship before the task: ask how someone is and wait for the answer. Daily micro-tasks delivered by app changed chosen traits, and observers saw the increases.
Each week, ask for one view that contradicts yours and write down what is right about it. Treat this as a completed challenge; change followed challenges done, not challenges chosen.

ESFJ.line: Sociable and considerate, keeps groups running smoothly and values tradition.

growth.text: Add one new experience a week that is yours alone, such as a talk, a gallery or an unfamiliar subject. Openness goals were among those people chose and moved in the PEACH trial, though Openness is harder to shift than other traits.
The MBTI does not measure how much you worry about others' approval. If your Big Five Neuroticism score here is high, that is the most changeable trait in intervention research and a good first goal.

ISTP.line: Calm and practical, learns by doing and likes to understand how things work.

growth.text: Complete one small weekly challenge that involves telling someone what you are thinking, such as explaining a decision out loud. Extraversion rose with the number of challenges completed.
Use if-then plans for the dull parts: 'If I finish a job, then I log it before starting the next.' Concrete plans beat general intentions over 16 weeks.

ISFP.line: Gentle and observant, lives in the present and expresses things through what they make or do.

growth.text: Set one if-then plan for the week ahead: 'If it is Sunday evening, then I write my three priorities.' If-then planning was what helped people become more conscientious when they wanted to.
Share one piece of work or one opinion with someone new each week and record it. Small completed social challenges predicted higher Extraversion.

ESTP.line: Energetic and direct, acts first and adjusts as things happen.

growth.text: Take one weekly challenge that delays a reward, such as finishing paperwork before the fun task. Conscientiousness increased for those who completed such challenges and dipped for those who skipped them.
For three months, do one small considerate act a day that nobody asked for. Daily tasks through a coaching app produced changes that other people could see.

ESFP.line: Lively and generous, enjoys people and makes ordinary moments fun.

growth.text: Make an if-then plan for money or deadlines: 'If I am paid, then I move 10% to savings the same day.' Specific plans were the difference between wanting to change and changing.
Spend 15 minutes a day for three months on one subject you know nothing about. Short daily tasks moved Openness goals in the PEACH trial, though expect a smaller shift than for other traits.
